## Example

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Choose a one-oscillator Lorentz response with $\varepsilon_\infty>0$ in $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$, $a>0$ in $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$, $\omega_0>0$ and $\gamma>0$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and fix $\omega>0$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. In the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention its scalar absolute permittivity is $\varepsilon(\omega)=\varepsilon_\infty+a/(\omega_0^2-\omega^2-i\gamma\omega)$. Let $I_3$ denote the $3\times3$ identity matrix, and let the tensor coefficients be $\boldsymbol\varepsilon(\omega)=\varepsilon(\omega)I_3$ and $\boldsymbol\mu=\mu I_3$ with real $\mu>0$ in $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$. These coefficients satisfy the transpose-symmetry condition of the reciprocal phasor model, while $\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon(\omega)>0$. For any nonzero local electric amplitude $e\in\mathbb C^3$ in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, define the real electric field at a fixed material point by $E(t)=\operatorname{Re}(e e^{-i\omega t})$. Let $p_1=(\varepsilon(\omega)-\varepsilon_\infty)e$ be the oscillator polarization amplitude from the one-oscillator response, in $\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}$; put $P_1(t)=\operatorname{Re}(p_1e^{-i\omega t})$, and define its polarization-current contribution by $J_{\mathrm{osc}}(t):=\partial_tP_1(t)$. Its phasor amplitude is $j_{\mathrm{osc}}=-i\omega(\varepsilon(\omega)-\varepsilon_\infty)e$ in $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$. The cycle-averaged work density of this oscillator-current contribution on the electric field, in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$, is

$$\overline q_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac1T\int_0^T J_{\mathrm{osc}}(t)\cdot E(t)\,dt=\frac{\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon(\omega)|e|^2>0,\qquad T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega},\qquad |e|^2:=e^*\cdot e=\sum_{r=1}^3|e_r|^2.$$

Here $e^*$ is componentwise complex conjugation. The conjugate used in this cycle average is distinct from the bilinear, unconjugated product in the reciprocity identity.

Thus the coefficient condition that supplies the Lorentz reciprocity identity is compatible with positive cycle-averaged work on the oscillator-current contribution in this adopted model.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a single Lorentz oscillator with the strictly positive coefficients and damping specified above, a fixed real $\omega>0$, real scalar $\mu>0$, and a nonzero local harmonic electric amplitude $e$.

[A1] $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is explicitly assumed by the supplier statement used for the oscillator response ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F1] For the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention and one Lorentz oscillator driven by electric-field amplitude $e$, the oscillator polarization amplitude is $p_1=a e/(\omega_0^2-\omega^2-i\gamma\omega)=(\varepsilon(\omega)-\varepsilon_\infty)e$. Also $\varepsilon(\omega)=\varepsilon_\infty+a/(\omega_0^2-\omega^2-i\gamma\omega)$ and $\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon(\omega)=a\gamma\omega/((\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+\gamma^2\omega^2)\ge0$ ([[pthm-emx-lorentz-susceptibility]], harmonic-response calculation and pointwise-loss clause).

[F2] The phasor medium is reciprocal exactly when $\boldsymbol\varepsilon^T=\boldsymbol\varepsilon$ and $\boldsymbol\mu^T=\boldsymbol\mu$; its products in the Lorentz identity are bilinear without conjugation ([[def-emx-reciprocal-phasor-medium]]).

[L1] Two C1 phasor solutions of the reciprocal model obey the bounded-domain Lorentz bilinear identity; the theorem does not require the coefficients to be Hermitian or lossless ([[pthm-emx-lorentz-reciprocity]]).

## Verification

1.1 The denominator $(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+\gamma^2\omega^2$ is strictly positive because $\gamma\omega>0$. Therefore [F1] gives $\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon(\omega)=a\gamma\omega/((\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+\gamma^2\omega^2)>0$. A scalar multiple of $I_3$ equals its ordinary transpose even when the scalar is complex, and the real scalar $\mu$ also equals its transpose; hence [F2] places these coefficients in the reciprocal class. The reciprocity identity [L1] is consequently applicable whenever the corresponding C1 phasor solutions exist. [given, A1, F1, F2, L1, algebra]

2.1 By [F1], $P_1(t)=\operatorname{Re}(p_1e^{-i\omega t})$ has amplitude $p_1=(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_\infty)e$, so $J_{\mathrm{osc}}=\partial_tP_1$ has phasor amplitude $j_{\mathrm{osc}}=-i\omega p_1$. For any complex scalar amplitudes $u,v$, write the product as $\frac14(uv e^{-2i\omega t}+uv^*+u^*v+u^*v^*e^{2i\omega t})$. The period integrals of $e^{\pm2i\omega t}$ are zero because $\omega>0$, so the average is $\frac12\operatorname{Re}(uv^*)$. Applying this componentwise gives $\overline q_{\mathrm{osc}}=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(j_{\mathrm{osc}}\cdot e^*)=\frac{\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_\infty)|e|^2=\frac{\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon|e|^2>0$, since $\varepsilon_\infty$ is real and $e\ne0$. Positive $\overline q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is work transferred from the field to the oscillator-current contribution in the adopted Maxwell sign convention. This is a model deduction, not an observation. [given, A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

This calculation establishes coexistence of transpose-symmetric reciprocal coefficients and positive cycle-averaged work on the oscillator-current contribution in the stated model. It makes no claim about a time-reversal transformation.
